title: Nineveh turns (Jonah 3)
hookLine: the enemy city repents, down to the cattle, and God relents

lines: THE WORD CAME THE SECOND TIME.
ONE DAY INTO A THREE-DAY CITY.
cards: Chapter three opens with a line almost funny in its patience. In the King James Bible: "And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time." The second time.
Same message, same city, as if the storm and the fish were a long detour. This time Jonah goes. Nineveh is huge, the story says, a city of three days' journey.
Jonah walks one day in and delivers a sermon so short it barely counts. In Hebrew it's five words. In English: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown."
No call to repent. No promise of mercy. Just the warning.

teach.b: "So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them." The great city of the empire Israel feared turns, all of it, and fast.

teach.h: THE KING IN SACKCLOTH AND ASH.
teach.b: The king gets up off his throne, takes off his robe, puts on sackcloth and sits in the ash. His decree: no person and no animal is to eat or drink.
Cattle and sheep too, covered in sackcloth, crying out. It's a little comic, cows in mourning clothes, but it's also complete: the whole city, down to the barn.
The king's reasoning is humble: "Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?" Who can tell. He doesn't presume.
Then: "God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." And God relented and did not destroy them.
Jewish tradition calls this kind of turning teshuvah, coming back, and on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the book of Jonah is read aloud in synagogue. Christians in some churches hear it in Lent.
And some readers hear a quiet twist in Jonah's five words: the Hebrew for overthrown can also mean turned over, changed.

teach.h: WHO CAN TELL IF GOD WILL TURN?
teach.b: In forty days, Nineveh would be turned upside down. It was. Just not the way Jonah meant.

how: Some churches read Jonah 3 during Lent as a picture of repentance, and Jesus points to the people of Nineveh in Matthew 12:41 and Luke 11:32 as people who turned when they heard Jonah.

o: Jonah turns back and finally heads to the city
a feared city repents, from the king to the cattle
a feared city is destroyed by fire from heaven

games.q: who did what in Jonah 3 — tap the pairs.
p: walked one day in and warned
left his throne for sackcloth and ash

s: Jonah preached a long sermon calling Nineveh to repent
his whole message is five Hebrew words: forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.
the king ordered even the animals to fast
no person and no animal was to eat or drink, and the cattle wore sackcloth too.
the king was sure God would spare them
he only hoped: "who can tell if God will turn and repent."

games.q: you're the king of Nineveh, ruler of a feared empire. a foreign prophet walks in and says your city will be overthrown in forty days. what do you do?
o: take off your robe, sit in ashes, and call a fast.
games.why: the king rises from his throne, puts on sackcloth, sits in ash, and calls the whole city, animals included, to fast and turn. God relents.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've quietly written off, your own private Nineveh; you don't have to like them, or trust them yet. Ask the king's question, who can tell, and imagine for a few breaths that they might turn.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, leave the door to their changing open a crack.

wordCard.voice: Nineveh turns. The great enemy city hears five words and turns around, from the king to the cattle, and God relents.

orig.note: Hebrew: turning, return. the later Jewish word for repentance, the turning Nineveh does.

carryVoice: Your line: even nineveh. Who can tell, as the king asked? Rest well; there's more Jonah tomorrow.
